title: Quality policy, scope and measurable objectives
audience: Supervisors, leads and office staff who help write or follow a quality system for a commercial or housekeeping service.
learningOutcomes: Explain what a quality policy commits a business to and what it does not do.
Write a scope statement that names the services covered and any clause excluded, with a reason.
Turn a general quality aim into two objectives that can be measured.

instruction.heading: What a quality policy is for
instruction.body: A quality policy is a short statement of what the business promises its clients and staff. The sample manual commits the firm to meeting its own and its clients' expectations, to forming lasting ties with customers, to improving its systems, to using its resources well and to complying with the laws that apply to it. A policy is a commitment, not a procedure. The procedures sit beneath it and must support what the policy says. A policy that nobody can act on is a notice on a wall.

instruction.heading: Scope and exclusions
instruction.body: The scope marks out which services the system governs. In the sample, the services listed are janitorial work, laundry, pest control and general housekeeping. It also records one excluded clause, the one covering design and development, because the firm offers no new services. An exclusion is only valid if the reason holds. If the business starts a new service, the excluded clause must be brought back in. Write the scope so a new supervisor can tell at a glance whether a service is covered.

instruction.heading: Objectives that can be measured
instruction.body: The sample sets objectives such as reducing client complaints, improving margin and stabilising the customer base. These are useful aims, but an objective needs a measure, a date and an owner before it can be checked. Turning 'reduce complaints' into 'log every complaint for three months and compare the count with the prior three months' gives a result that can be shown to the management review. The sample also notes that the customer decides what quality means, so feedback from clients should shape the objectives.

instruction.heading: Standards named in the sample
instruction.body: The sample states that it applies a version of an international quality standard. Its figures and retention periods come from a 2012 sample for a non-Australian operation, so they are not Australian facts. Confirm the current edition of any standard before naming it in a business document.

procedure: Read the business's quality policy and list the commitments it makes to clients and to staff.
Write the scope as a list of covered services, with any excluded clause and a one-line reason.
Choose three aims from the policy and rewrite each as an objective with a measure, a date and an owner.
Check each objective against client feedback received in the last quarter.
Record the signed policy, scope and objectives with a review date.

workedExamples.situation: A housekeeping firm is starting a turnover service for short-stay apartments. Its scope document excludes design and development because the firm offered no new services.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the excluded clause stay in the scope, and what objective would show the new service is working?
workedExamples.reasoning: The reason for the exclusion no longer holds, so the scope must be updated and the clause brought back in. A suitable objective is to record the checklist score for each new turnover job over the first month, with the supervisor as owner and a review date set.

equipmentAndPpe: No specialist equipment. A copy of the business's policy and scope document.

commonErrors.error: Writing a quality policy that makes promises no procedure can deliver.
commonErrors.prevention: Check each commitment against a named procedure or record.

commonErrors.error: Excluding a clause and never reviewing the reason.
commonErrors.prevention: Write the reason beside the exclusion and review it when services change.

commonErrors.error: Setting objectives with no measure or owner.
commonErrors.prevention: Give every objective a measure, a date and a named owner.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: A quality policy that commits to complying with the law does not itself state what the law requires. Check the applicable requirements for the business. Its figures and retention periods come from a 2012 sample for a non-Australian operation, so they are not Australian facts.

qualityStandard: The scope lists each covered service and gives a reason for every exclusion.
Each objective has a measure, a date and an owner.
documentationEvidence: Signed quality policy with a review date.
Scope statement with exclusions and reasons.
Objectives register with owner and measure.
summary: A quality policy is a commitment, supported by procedures.
A scope exclusion must have a reason and is reviewed when services change.
An objective needs a measure, a date and an owner before it can be checked.

knowledgeChecks.question: What is a quality policy best described as?
options: A detailed step-by-step cleaning method for each room
A short statement of commitments that procedures must support
A staff roster that lists shifts and leave for each week
A list of suppliers and their contact details and prices

knowledgeChecks.question: When is an excluded clause in a scope statement valid?
options: Once it is written down, with no reason given
Only when the stated reason still holds
Only when a client asks for it

knowledgeChecks.question: Which objective can be checked in practice?
options: Be the best cleaning firm in the whole city and be known for it by everyone
Keep clients happy through friendly phone calls each week and send a card at each holiday
Improve quality over time for every single client across the whole city
Log every complaint for three months and compare the count with the prior three months
